articles.description: Federal prosecutors moved to drop their case against David Hearn, blaming Reflecting Pool damage on a "botched installation" rather than vandalism. That has implications for others who were charged.
articles.title: Ripple effects: Three people have Reflecting Pool charges dropped after Hearn request

articles.author: Will Stone
articles.description: An FDA advisory panel recently voted to green-light some popular peptides. The decision brought enormous attention to the market for these products — and concerns about the unregulated supply.
articles.title: What would it take to get peptides on the shelf?

articles.description: Tens of millions of Americans have criminal records that can be barriers to employment. An AI-powered app is helping those eligible to expunge their records at a pace not seen before.
articles.title: For those with criminal records, AI is breaking down barriers to employment

Murray Watt, the federal environment minister, was asked earlier about former rugby league star Luke Bateman’s testimony before a parliamentary inquiry on gambling reform.
Bateman alleged betting company promoters supplied him with cocaine and alcohol, also alleging he attended private Gold Coast events hosted by gambling firms where senior figures took illegal drugs with clients.
We all feel for him and the circumstances that he went through. And for anyone to be offering illegal drugs as an inducement or for any other reason is obviously a crime. Should not be committed and people should pay a price if they’re engaging in that kind of criminal behavior.

articles.title: Australia news live: St Kilda may lose hundreds of little penguins to bird flu; corruption inquiry told of $50,000 branch stacking scheme

articles.description:
Former 2UE and 2GB radio broadcaster is facing 22 charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty

Jones allegedly gifted cash and car to teenager he kissed after commenting on sprinter’s penis, trial hears

He told the court that before this visit he had done “whatever I could to not go there on my own”.

articles.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: former radio broadcaster in Sydney court for day two of indecent assault case – latest news

articles.author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
articles.description:
Betting firms respond to claims made by anti-gambling campaigners Tim Costello and Luke Bateman at parliamentary inquiry
Betting giants Sportsbet and Tabcorp say there is no evidence to substantiate allegations that account managers sourced drugs and sex workers to incentivise vulnerable people to bet more, calling for information about the claims to be provided to regulators.
The anti-gambling campaigners Tim Costello and Luke Bateman used a parliamentary hearing into Labor’s legislation to curb gambling advertising to allege problem gamblers had been supplied with cocaine, alcohol and sex workers, alleging companies exercised no duty of care to their customers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sportsbet and Tabcorp deny allegations they sourced drugs and sex workers to encourage VIP clients to bet more

articles.author: Abené Clayton
articles.description:
Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, was arrested in New Jersey in June, and died after a ‘medical emergency’, agency said
An immigrant being held at a New Jersey ICE detention center died on 1 August, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on Monday. Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, is the 22nd person to die in ICE custody this year, according to agency data.
Lopez-Cornejo, who is originally from El Salvador and first came to the US in 2006, was arrested by ICE agents in Plainfield, New Jersey, on 18 June and sent to Delaney Hall detention facility to await deportation. Less than two months later he suffered an unspecified “medical emergency”, and was later pronounced dead by University Hospital in Newark, New Jersey, ICE said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Immigrant being held at Delaney Hall dies, marking 22nd death in ICE custody

articles.author: Coral Murphy Marcos, Joseph Gedeon, Maya Yang, Shrai Popat and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Sign up for the US Breaking News email

On Tuesday, we’ll bring you the latest from Michigan where voters will head to the polls for competitive primaries in Senate and House races.
The most closely watched competition is the Democratic primary for the US Senate, where congresswoman Haley Stevens is up against former public health official Abdul El-Sayed. They’re vying to ultimately win the seat of outgoing senator Gary Peters in November. The race has now turned into a proxy battle for the future of the Democratic party. Establishment-backed Stevens has received support from party leaders and her race has been buoyed by millions from the pro-Israel lobby. Meanwhile the insurgent El-Sayed has built a strong grassroots movement and is endorsed by progressives lawmakers in the Democratic caucus.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump declines to call for Max Miller’s resignation amid abuse allegations – as it happened

articles.author: Coral Murphy Marcos and agencies
articles.description:
Residents and farmers say contractors have tapped border aquifers that threaten water supply for those nearby
Construction crews building a border wall in New Mexico were ordered to stop drilling new wells after ranchers said that pumping groundwater to produce concrete could threaten their livestock amid a severe drought.
The order comes as crews across the southern border race to complete one of Donald Trump’s highest domestic priorities – barriers that span four states and received over $46bn in federal funding. Controversies have sprouted up in Texas and California, and border-town residents and environmentalists have reported a wide variety of issues with construction.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Crews building Trump border wall in drought-hit New Mexico ordered to stop drilling wells

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Prime minister Sanae Takaichi visited Kumamoto prefecture almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 quake hit, killing 38 people
Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has visited the south-western prefecture of Kumamoto, where recovery efforts are being hampered by heat and a lack of water supplies, almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake killed dozens and caused widespread damage.
Thirty-eight people died during the quake, including one person who died of apparent heatstroke while taking shelter in a car in hot weather, officials said on Monday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Japan’s prime minister tours earthquake-hit sites as recovery efforts hampered by soaring temperatures

articles.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
articles.description:
Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback calls failure to pay Briana Whatley money owed ‘an oversight’
A far-right Republican candidate in Florida’s governor’s race has been accused of stiffing a high school debate champion over the better part of $11,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded.
Student Briana Whatley landed the awards as regional and national champion of Incubate Debate, a league-style competition set up by the candidate, James Fishback, to encourage youth to engage in political discourse.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Far-right Republican accused of stiffing student debate champion of $8,000

articles.author: Sam Levine and Chris Stein in Washington
articles.description:
Democrats say agreement – which clears way for Blanche’s confirmation – makes promises president can easily reverse
A compromise between Todd Blanche and two Republican senators that potentially cleared the way for Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general is weak, Democrats and several experts said, as it makes promises Donald Trump can easily reverse.
Blanche, the acting attorney general, posted two documents on Sunday evening showing he was withdrawing an 18 May order allowing for the creation of a $1.8bn weaponization fund and clarifying that broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Completely hollow’: critics denounce Blanche deal to halt Trump slush fund

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Shares soar as yearly revenue up 93%, even as opposition grows to company’s role in Trump immigration agenda
In a sea of companies reporting mixed financial results this quarter, Palantir stands out. Although Palantir was not immune to the AI jitters that caused industry-wide drops in share prices earlier this year, the AI and analytics company reported that its overall revenue grew 93% year over year to $1.94bn. That’s well over the $1.8bn Wall Street expected Palantir to bring in for the second quarter.
The glowing financials sparked a 10% surge in share prices in the immediate aftermath. Despite growing opposition to Palantir’s work with various governments including the crucial role the company plays in the Trump administration’s immigration agenda, Palantir’s revenue from US government contracts grew 90% year over year to $809m.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘This quarter was otherworldly’: Palantir earnings surge past expectations

articles.author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
articles.description:
Survey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staff
NHS radiographers are experiencing racist abuse by patients, who have called them “monkeys” and refused to be seen by black and Asian staff, according to a report.
A survey of 381 members of the Society of Radiographers revealed a “noticeable” rise in instances of overt racism experienced and witnessed by radiographers across the health service over the past 18 months.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS radiographers report rise in overt racist abuse by patients

articles.author: Pjotr Sauer and Angus Thomson
articles.description:
Seven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforce
Ukrainian drone attacks on a Black Sea resort and the annexed Crimea peninsula killed 11 people, Russian officials said after blaming Ukraine for another explosion that killed five people in a Moscow restaurant.
Seven people, including three children, were killed when “drone debris” struck a beach in the seaside town of Arkhipo-Osipovka, the crisis taskforce for Russia’s southern Krasnodar region said on social media.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claims

articles.author: Lucy Campbell (now); Angus Thomson, Tom Ambrose and Vivian Ho (earlier)
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.
People walk near a billboard depicting Iran’s late supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on a street in Tehran, Iran, earlier today.
Six Saudi-flagged supertankers have changed course in the Gulf of Aden in recent days amid threats from the Iran-aligned Houthis, Reuters reports.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump claims strait of Hormuz could open ‘by tomorrow’ as Iran denies any talks taking place – as it happened

articles.author: Rajeev Syal and Alexandra Topping
articles.description:
Andy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until October
Rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded from early release plans to ease critical prison overcrowding in a major intervention by Andy Burnham.
The prime minister said on Tuesday that he would delay the planned early release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales by a month until October.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rapists, child abusers and groomers will not leave prison early, says PM

articles.author: Helena Smith in Athens
articles.description:
Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing
Greek authorities are investigating what may have motivated a 26-year-old Afghan man to kill a Scottish charity worker found dead in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens last month.
Inquiries have focused increasingly on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s last few hours alive and police believe they hold the key to revealing why the 38-year-old was targeted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Athens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murder

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
New talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday.
Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait of Hormuz and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump says

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
Joshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP
A former neo-Nazi activist with convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP has been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election in Somerset.
Joshua Bonehill-Paine, the creator of the viral Crewkerne Gazette series of AI clips, is due to stand for election to Somerset council next year in a new Crewkerne South district. He told the Guardian he was an executive member of the Tories’ Yeovil branch, working as an events organiser.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Former neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council election

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
Restore leader has countered charges he’s splitting the right while showing his party is a very real obstacle for Reform
Even by the standards of their rivalry, the speed at which Rupert Lowe’s olive branch to Nigel Farage morphed into fresh recriminations between the two was swift.
It began with a softly lit 12-minute video posted on Sunday by the Restore Britain leader, looking straight to camera and referring to “Nigel” as he suggested his party could be willing to cast aside its differences with Reform UK and work together.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rupert Lowe’s ‘olive branch’ to Farage piles more pressure on Reform leader

articles.author: Andrew Roth
articles.description:
US president reduced to bemoaning Tehran’s ‘unbelievable duplicity’ as he struggles to find solid negotiating ground
The Donald Trump doctrine has always contained a tenuous relationship with the truth. It was his mentor, the infamous New York lawyer Roy Cohn, who taught the young real estate mogul always to claim victory and never to admit defeat. Unfortunately for Trump, in Iran the US president has found a counterpart just as stubborn as himself.
As Trump claims new negotiations are to begin with Tehran this week, Iran has shown it can also reignite the conflict by lobbing ballistic missiles at US bases in the region and maintaining a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz, effectively taking initiative in the stalled peace process. And time is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks toward a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump meets his obstinate match in Iran’s hardball regime

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Ruling quashes Home Office policy to refuse asylum seekers’ right to have trafficking claims reconsidered after initial rejection
A high court judge has ordered the Home Office to bring an alleged victim of trafficking forcibly removed to France under the “one in one out” scheme back to the UK.
It is the first ruling of its kind and could lead to more people affected by the “one in one out” policy being brought back to the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Judge orders return of alleged victim of trafficking sent to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.
In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Houghwith Ashifa Kassam; produced by Annie La Vespaand Bryony Moore; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin
articles.description:
Dozens of people died attempting to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after an estimated 50,000 crossed from Morocco last week. The incident has led to a political crisis in Spain and criticism from EU countries.
Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s European community affairs correspondent, Ashifa Kassam – watch on YouTube
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The Latest

articles.author: Pjotr Sauer
articles.description:
Boris Nadezhdin, who gained prominence after standing against Putin in 2024, says he is now in France
The prominent Russian anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin has fled to Paris as Moscow tightens its grip on dissent before parliamentary elections later this year.
Nadezhdin, a veteran liberal politician, gained international prominence during Russia’s 2024 presidential election when his long-shot campaign against Vladimir Putin unexpectedly gathered momentum before electoral authorities barred him from running.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anti-war politician flees Russia amid pre-election crackdown on dissent

articles.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
articles.description:
Internal inquiries also opened after two suicides and two attempted suicides of staff in departments connected to PM’s office
The Paris state prosecutor has opened a preliminary inquiry into alleged workplace bullying after the attempted suicide of a staff member in a department connected to the French prime minister’s office, France Inter radio has revealed.
The public radio station reported on Monday that two government workers in different departments had ended their lives in the past year, and two others had attempted suicide. The radio station said complaints of alleged workplace bullying had been made.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Paris prosecutor investigates alleged bullying in government departments after suicide attempt

articles.author: Josh Taylor Technology reporter
articles.description:
Expert says people face being filmed without their consent as $89 Anko smartglasses sell out in stores and online

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Kmart has sold out of Anko-branded $89 camera glasses across Australia, which a digital rights expert says presents a “privacy nightmare” as people face being filmed without their consent.
As of Monday, the clear-lens, black-rimmed glasses, which can capture images and record high-definition videos, were sold out at Kmart stores across Australia and online.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kmart sells out of low-cost rival to Meta camera glasses across Australia amid warnings of ‘privacy nightmare’

articles.author: Luca Ittimani
articles.description:
Handful of tollroads to get one-off price cuts but WestConnex toll to keep rising at least 4% a year

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The cost of using Sydney’s biggest toll road will continue to rise at least 4% a year after the multinational private operator was accused of blocking the state government’s push for sweeping reforms.
Only a handful of Sydney’s motorways will receive one-off toll cuts under a deal announced by the state Labor government on Monday, as the tolling bill footed by taxpayers surpasses $1bn.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Most Sydney road tolls to keep rising after Transurban accused of blocking reforms

articles.author: Jakub Krupa
articles.description:
Explosives used to move a large rock and let more water flow to cool nuclear power plant
More must be done ⁠to strengthen the European Union’s borders at critical points, ⁠European Commission president ⁠Ursula ​von der Leyen told Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez ⁠in a letter.
In the carefully-calibrated letter, first reported by Reuters and a number of Spanish media, von der Leyen was quoted as congratulating Spain for swiftly handling the incident and “successfully preventing” the onward migration to mainland Spain and the EU.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South-eastern Europe faces heatwave energy crunch as Romania detonates Danube rock to increase water flow – as it happened

articles.author: Ashifa Kassam in Madrid, Okba Mohammad in Ceuta and Lisa O’Carroll in London
articles.description:
Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity

Explainer: why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?

A growing chorus of voices has accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.
Spanish officials ⁠said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa, had returned to Morocco in recent days. About 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing

articles.author: Natasha May in Bangkok
articles.description:
Meeting follows years of questions over wellbeing of detained former leader, who was ousted by coup in 2021
Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi has met a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the aid organisation has confirmed.
The meeting on Monday ⁠followed years of questions over the wellbeing of the 81-year-old, whose whereabouts and health condition have been largely unknown since the elected civilian government she led was ousted by a military coup in February 2021.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Red Cross visits Aung San Suu Kyi after Myanmar military pushed to prove she is alive

articles.author: Andrew Roth and Sufian Taha in Turmus Ayya, West Bank. Photography by Quique Kierszenbaum
articles.description:
After visits by US ambassador Mike Huckabee to the nearby Israeli settlement of Shilo, Palestinian Americans in Turmus Ayya have witnessed a terrifying rise in attacks
No man’s land in Turmus Ayya lies where the US flags end and the Israeli flags begin. It is a few hundred metres of soil scorched by molotov cocktails where Israeli settlers have placed a boulder to tell the Palestinian villagers: this is our land now.
On one side of that boulder are the white-stoned mansions where the Palestinian residents of Turmus Ayya live. About 80% of them are US citizens, members of the diaspora in New York, Chicago and Paterson, New Jersey, who return for the summers and bring their children here to experience Palestinian culture and learn Arabic. Many call themselves proud American patriots and fly the stars and stripes from their balconies.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Abandoned by the US: Palestinian Americans trapped in a surge of Israeli settler violence

articles.author: Associated Press in Wellington
articles.description:
Pacific nation is latest country to signal a shift away from its colonial past with return to its traditional name
The Pacific Island country of Nauru has changed its name to the Republic of Naoero, its president said, matching the spelling and pronunciation in the national language.
The country’s international code will change from NRU to NRO and its people will be known as dei-Naoero instead of Nauruan. Commonly known abroad by the pronunciation of Now-roo, the new name is spoken as Now-ero.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nauru officially changes its name to Naoero

articles.author: Graeme Wearden
articles.description:
US and Japanese governments confirm they carried out a rare joint intervention late last week

Why has Trump stepped in to prop up Japan’s currency?

Business live – latest updates

The yen has hit its highest level in three months after Japan and the US launched a combined operation to support the Japanese currency.
The yen strengthened to ¥155 to the US dollar on Monday, its highest level since early May, after Tokyo and Washington confirmed they had carried out a rare joint currency intervention late last week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Yen hits three-month high after Trump helps prop up currency

articles.author: Ed Walton for MetDesk
articles.description:
Soaring temperatures continue to sweep parts of Europe, while Okinawa faces powerful winds and storm surges

Europe live – latest updates

Unbearable, record-breaking heat has dominated the summer of 2026 across much of Europe. New records were set in central Europe last week, with Wieselburg in Austria registering a new July peak of 40.3C (104.5F). This is particularly significant as it is just 0.2C behind the all-time high, set in the August of 2003.
However, not all of the northern hemisphere has experienced extreme heat and aridity. Vancouver recorded its wettest July since 2016 and the third wettest since 2008, with 33.6mm of rain. While that total may not appear exceptional, it is only a touch above the 1991-2020 climate average, highlighting how unusually dry July has been in the Canadian city over the past decade.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Weather tracker: Austria breaks heat records as Japan braces for Typhoon Dolphin

articles.author: Mark Saunokonoko
articles.description:
Authorities issue alert saying indoor spaces without airconditioning are ‘dangerous’ as temperatures pass 40C for fifth straight day 
South Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, as authorities warned people to “immediately” stop all outdoor activities in affected areas.
The south-eastern city of Yangsan saw the temperature reach 42.5C on Sunday afternoon, the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said, the highest temperature reported since modern weather observation began in 1904.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Stop all outdoor activities’: South Korea records its highest ever temperature

articles.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
articles.description:
Passing of bill technically gives English same status as Māori and sign language but, with it already spoken by 95% of country, critics call it ‘a pointless exercise’
Legislation recognising English as an official language of New Zealand has been passed by parliament, prompting derision from linguists and legal experts and a now-viral broadside from a Māori MP who called it “pathetic”.
The English language bill became law on 30 July giving English, which is spoken by 95% of the country, the same official status as te reo Māori (Māori language) and New Zealand sign language. However, experts say it is already considered an official language as a result of usage and custom.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Zealand legislation recognising English an official language ridiculed as ‘pathetic’

articles.author: Okba Mohammad and Javier Jennings Mozo in Ceuta
articles.description:
People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects
Four days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum from Morocco to the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain.
Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return to Spain, from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Activists in the region say politicians regard LGBTQ+ people as ‘the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power’
A growing number of west African countries are implementing or strengthening anti-LGBTQ+ laws, amid local political pressures and a global pushback against LGBTQ+ rights.
In March, Senegal doubled the maximum prison sentence for gay sex to 10 years and criminalised the “promotion” of homosexuality. Niger criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February, the first time same-sex intimacy had been outlawed in the country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anti-LGBTQ+ laws are on the rise across west Africa, campaigners warn

articles.author: Dan Collyns in Lima
articles.description:
Aircraft crashes into field after departing from nearby city of Pisco, according to local authorities
Police in Peru report that 13 people, among them foreign tourists, have been killed in a plane crash in southern Peru, near the Nazca Lines.
Local authorities in Nazca confirmed that 11 tourists and two pilots died when the Cessna Grand Caravan crashed in Pueblo Viejo, approximately 4 miles (6km) from the city of Nazca and roughly 12km from the Nazca Lines site.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13

articles.author: Geneva Abdul
articles.description:
Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak also died, climbing company says
A world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member has died after being among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.
Nirmal Purja was killed leading an expedition of 10 other people on the world’s 12th-highest mountain when an avalanche struck at around noon on Thursday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Top mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in Pakistan

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
António Guterres says strengthening El Niño will help push the world’s climate crisis into ‘uncharted territory’
India’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of the world as a stronger El Niño weather system is taking hold, weather experts have warned.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the strengthening El Niño was “adding fuel to a planet already on fire” and pushing the world into “uncharted territory”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s monsoon rains in danger as UN chief warns planet is ‘on fire’

articles.author: Hannah Harris Green in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
Injectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwide

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email 

New innovations in HIV prevention could dramatically reduce the number of new HIV cases around the globe, but US foreign aid cuts will mean that those that most need the new medication will be unable to access it, according to experts at the Aids 2026 Conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
One year ago, the World Health Organization recommended that governments around the world prioritize expanded access to lenacapavir, an injectable version of the HIV prevention medication PrEP that requires only two injections annually. PrEP, which also comes in the form of daily oral medications and bimonthly injections, is 99% effective in preventing sexually transmitted HIV for people who take it consistently.

articles.title: HIV prevention drug could reduce cases globally but USAID cuts prevent access, say experts

articles.description:
Rescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descent
The world-renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja – a former British special forces member – is among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.
The Alpine Club of Pakistan said “seven climbers have been spotted via aerial drone footage” adding that “their identities and condition cannot yet be verified”.

articles.title: World-renowned climber Nirmal Purja among 11 struck by avalanche on Pakistan mountain

articles.author: Olivia Bowden in Toronto
articles.description:
Data shows Canadians have replaced US vacations with other international trips in apparent rebuke to Trump
Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to the US in 2025 than in the previous year, as Donald Trump’s hostile policies towards his northern neighbour continue to incur an economic cost, new government data shows.
The research also indicates that Canadians are not bucking travel overall and instead have replaced US vacations with other international destinations, in a rebuke to Trump’s tariff regime and the president’s continued musings on annexing Canada.
 Continue reading...

Local civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackout
At least 30 people are alleged to have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in the past two days as part of what has been claimed is a brutal state crackdown that has engulfed the disputed region for weeks.
According to a local civil society group, Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the Pakistani security services fired on tens of thousands of peaceful protesters, killing 25 people on Monday and five more on Tuesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in Kashmir

articles.description:
Three years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study says
A spate of ferocious wildfires across North America and Europe, worsened by the climate crisis, has incinerated homes and forests and forced thousands of people to flee. Previous fires suggest the effects of these blazes may linger for years to come.
The current fires and their plumes of smoke can appear to be a temporary, if immediate, crisis.  Continue reading...
articles.title: Past fires suggest effects of Europe and North America wildfires may linger for years

articles.author: Coral Murphy Marcos, Joseph Gedeon, Maya Yang, Shrai Popat and Tom Ambrose

This live blog is now closed.

articles.description:
Residents and farmers say contractors have tapped border aquifers that threaten water supply for those nearby
Construction crews building a border wall in New Mexico were ordered to stop drilling new wells after ranchers said that pumping groundwater to produce concrete could threaten their livestock amid a severe drought.
The order comes as crews across the southern border race to complete one of Donald Trump’s highest domestic priorities – barriers that span four states and received over $46bn in federal funding. Controversies have sprouted up in Texas and California, and border-town residents and environmentalists have reported a wide variety of issues with construction.

articles.description:
Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback calls failure to pay Briana Whatley money owed ‘an oversight’
A far-right Republican candidate in Florida’s governor’s race has been accused of stiffing a high school debate champion over the better part of $11,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded.
Student Briana Whatley landed the awards as regional and national champion of Incubate Debate, a league-style competition set up by the candidate, James Fishback, to encourage youth to engage in political discourse.

articles.title: Far-right Republican accused of stiffing student debate champion of $8,000

articles.author: Sam Levine and Chris Stein in Washington
articles.description:
Democrats say agreement – which clears way for Blanche’s confirmation – makes promises president can easily reverse
A compromise between Todd Blanche and two Republican senators that potentially cleared the way for Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general is weak, Democrats and several experts said, as it makes promises Donald Trump can easily reverse.
Blanche, the acting attorney general, posted two documents on Sunday evening showing he was withdrawing an 18 May order allowing for the creation of a $1.8bn weaponization fund and clarifying that broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses.

articles.description:
North Carolina congressman’s campaign rejects committee finding that Edwards ‘engaged in sexual harassment’
The US House of Representatives ethics committee on Monday recommended that Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman, face censure after determining he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers.
The bipartisan panel began investigating the second-term North Carolina congressman earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, they determined there “was substantial reason to believe” Edwards broke House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees.
 Continue reading...

Democrats are pissed off – and they're taking their anger straight to the ballot box. In the wake of Donald Trump's return to the White House, progressives (including members of DSA – Democratic Socialists of America) have defeated established moderates in elections in liberal cities like New York, Washington DC and Seattle. Now, they're trying to win a series of major primaries in the deep-purple midwest. Host Carter Sherman speaks with Guardian midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang, who has traveled all over the region covering several key races – including this week's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, where progressive Abdul Al-Sayed is squaring off against the establishment candidate, Haley Stevens. Can leftist politics win outside of blue bubbles? And what do these races reveal about the fight for the midterms and the White House?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mamdani won New York. Can a progressive win the Michigan primary? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

The Greeks learn at Troy that breaking the rules works, then carry the lesson home. Nolan’s film shows how an exception becomes a habit of power

This article contains spoilers for The Odyssey

I had not read The Odyssey since I was a student. Stories change when we return to them later in life, or perhaps we are the ones who change. Christopher Nolan’s film made me want to find out what I had missed.
More specifically, it made me want to read Emily Wilson’s translation. Her scathing essay about the film nearly stopped me from buying her translation. I bought the book anyway.

articles.title: Nolan’s Odyssey shows what happens when a leader’s violations are rewarded | Jamil Smith

articles.author: Victoria Bekiempis

After the justice department botched file rollout under the original act, lawmakers now want legislation with teeth 
As Jeffrey Epstein survivors and their supporters continue searching for justice and transparency in the US, a bipartisan group of politicians is trying to rework legislation that heralded the release of long-hidden investigative files on the scandal.
While the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), signed into law by Donald Trump on 19 November, mandated that the justice department release all investigative files within 30 days with limited exceptions, survivors and their supporters have repeatedly grappled with missed deadlines and what they say are incomplete disclosures.
 Continue reading...

articles.author: Chris Stein in St Louis, Missouri
articles.description:
Voters face a choice of progressive ex-congresswoman Cori Bush or pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell on Tuesday
The pastor of a historically Black church on St Louis’s north side, Rodrick Burton, has watched with bewilderment as the congressional race in his district has drawn national attention not about the bloodshed in his community, but rather in Gaza.
“As a pastor who’s had eight members murdered, violence over there is terrible,” Burton said of the conflict in the Middle East.

articles.title: Will Missouri be the next primary win for a democratic socialist challenger?

articles.author: Jan-Werner Müller
articles.description:
The president’s methods, from ‘flooding the zone’ with scandals to prioritizing loyalty over competence, could ultimately weaken rather than strengthen him
The pattern is by now all too familiar: with every power grab Trump tries – from a fraudulent speech about voter fraud to appeals to his supreme court to let him rig the midterms – a debate kicks off about whether these moves are signs of strength or of desperation. Maybe we keep getting caught in this debate because the question is badly posed. So much of what is distinctive about Trump’s governance during his second term can serve the consolidation of an autocratic regime and at the same time create particular vulnerabilities for the regime. We have to become better at identifying these weaknesses, as opposed to being shellshocked by Trump’s brazenness every single time.
Aspiring autocrats operate differently in the 21st century; in previous eras, they had little hesitation about unleashing violence and committing massive human rights violations. Today, they try to fool both domestic and international audiences into thinking that democracy and the rule of law still exist. The recently deposed Hungarian prime minister, Viktor Orbán, was a master of this technique; he spent many years performing what he called “the peacock dance” to convince the European Commission (and Chancellor Angela Merkel) that he wasn’t creating a kleptocratic autocracy.
Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Are Trump’s most blatant authoritarian moves backfiring? | Jan-Werner Müller

articles.author: Andrew Roth and Sufian Taha in Turmus Ayya, West Bank. Photography by Quique Kierszenbaum
articles.description:
After visits by US ambassador Mike Huckabee to the nearby Israeli settlement of Shilo, Palestinian Americans in Turmus Ayya have witnessed a terrifying rise in attacks
No man’s land in Turmus Ayya lies where the US flags end and the Israeli flags begin. It is a few hundred metres of soil scorched by molotov cocktails where Israeli settlers have placed a boulder to tell the Palestinian villagers: this is our land now.
On one side of that boulder are the white-stoned mansions where the Palestinian residents of Turmus Ayya live. About 80% of them are US citizens, members of the diaspora in New York, Chicago and Paterson, New Jersey, who return for the summers and bring their children here to experience Palestinian culture and learn Arabic. Many call themselves proud American patriots and fly the stars and stripes from their balconies.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Abandoned by the US: Palestinian Americans trapped in a surge of Israeli settler violence

articles.author: Edward Helmore
articles.description:
Convicted killer seeks to withdraw guilty plea and go to trial – but that could put death penalty sentence back in play
Could Bryan Kohberger, convicted 13 months ago of the murders of four University of Idaho students, now find himself on death row? That’s one potential outcome of a perplexing petition he filed last week in which he claimed he was misled by his defense attorneys into pleading guilty.
A new trial could grant the wishes of family members who hoped to see the 31-year doctoral criminology student convicted by a jury in open court and sentenced to death. Or is Kohberger simply following the example of many mass murderers in attempting to gain control of the narrative and extend the suffering of his victims’ families?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘He’s a narcissist’: could Idaho killer Bryan Kohberger win a new trial?

articles.author: Timothy Garton Ash
articles.description:
American democrats need a Hungarian-style landslide to overwhelm Trump’s attempts to rig November’s midterm elections
In these days of extreme weather events, it seems odd to say that the US needs a big landslide. But a landslide defeat for President Donald Trump in November’s midterm elections is exactly what is required if the country is to start reversing his deliberate and rapid erosion of its democracy.
The respected Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Institute at Gothenburg University argues that in 2025 the US saw one of the most rapid declines in liberal democracy on record. “Democracy in the USA,” says its Democracy Report 2026, “is now at its worst in 60 years.” As the imperial republic marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, the danger seen at the very beginning of its constitutional order by anti-federalists such as Patrick Henry – that of an overmighty president abusing his executive power in an attempt to become a new king – has come closer than ever before.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton Ash

articles.description:
With Republicans' chances in the midterms looking shaky, Donald Trump is increasingly trying to rewrite the rules that govern US elections. Voting rights groups say he's really laying the groundwork to suppress voters. Trump has already moved to change mail-in voting, but he now wants Congress to pass the Save America Act, which includes strict voter ID restrictions. He's also accused China of interfering in the 2020 election. (Trump didn't back up that claim with evidence.) Host Kai Wright speaks with Garrett Epps, legal affairs editor at Washington Monthly, about the threat to US elections and what voters can do to protect them.

Read Garrett Epps' story in Washington Monthly

 Continue reading...

articles.author: Judith Levine
articles.description:
Trump’s campaign of repression echoes the red scare. But now the government has bigger ambitions and more powerful tools
There are many parallels between the first McCarthy era, roughly 1946 to 1956, and Trump’s campaign of political repression, his own updated McCarthyism.
Both regimes crafted a monster of quasi-facts and innuendo and fed it with fear: an enemy within, well-organized and financed, secretive and violent, allied with evil foreigners and bent on overthrowing capitalism, democracy and Christian morality. Both used flagrantly unconstitutional means to cleanse the nation of the spectral menace.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: McCarthyism has returned to the United States – and this time it’s even more dangerous | Judith Levine

articles.description:
Earlier this year, Congress reached a depressing milestone: 86% of Americans, a record high, disapproved of its job performance. But this summer, there have been some signs that shifts are underway. On the left, House Democrats have just voted in unprecedented numbers to withhold military aid from Israel, and across the country, progressive candidates are running competitive primary campaigns that are energizing a base fed up with the status quo. On the right, Republicans are reeling from the sudden death of Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina senator and one of Donald Trump's staunchest supporters. Mitch McConnell, the former Senate majority leader, remains sequestered following a health scare in June, raising questions of if a changing of the guard might be underway there, too. Kai Wright and Carter Sherman are joined by David Smith, the Guardian's Washington bureau chief and Rachel Leingang, midwest political correspondent, to discuss gerontocracy, transparency, the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America and just how much of an inflection point this summer might be for both parties

articles.title: Is US Congress finally on the verge of a change? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Anna Isaac; produced by Natalie Ktena, Eleanor Biggs, Saskia Collette, Nilufer Aumeerally and Ross Burns; executive producers Sami Kent and Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
Reform UK’s finances have come under scrutiny like never before. What do we know about the party’s funding – and why do so many awkward questions remain for Nigel Farage? Anna Isaac explains
For a while this year, it looked like nothing could stop Nigel Farage getting to Downing Street. Not the allegations of schoolboy racism, not the dodgy Cameo videos or even the £400,000 he trousered for advertising gold bullion.
But at the end of April, the Guardian’s City editor, Anna Isaac, delivered a game-changing scoop. That Farage had been given a £5m gift, as he termed it, from the cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harbourne.

articles.description:

NHS radiographers are experiencing racist abuse by patients, who have called them “monkeys” and refused to be seen by black and Asian staff, according to a report.
A survey of 381 members of the Society of Radiographers revealed a “noticeable” rise in instances of overt racism experienced and witnessed by radiographers across the health service over the past 18 months.

Andy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until October
Rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded from early release plans to ease critical prison overcrowding in a major intervention by Andy Burnham.
The prime minister said on Tuesday that he would delay the planned early release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales by a month until October.

articles.title: Rapists, child abusers and groomers will not leave prison early, says PM

articles.author: Helena Smith in Athens
articles.description:
Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing
Greek authorities are investigating what may have motivated a 26-year-old Afghan man to kill a Scottish charity worker found dead in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens last month.
Inquiries have focused increasingly on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s last few hours alive and police believe they hold the key to revealing why the 38-year-old was targeted.

articles.title: Athens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murder

Joshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP
A former neo-Nazi activist with convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP has been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election in Somerset.
Joshua Bonehill-Paine, the creator of the viral Crewkerne Gazette series of AI clips, is due to stand for election to Somerset council next year in a new Crewkerne South district. He told the Guardian he was an executive member of the Tories’ Yeovil branch, working as an events organiser.

articles.title: Former neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council election

Restore leader has countered charges he’s splitting the right while showing his party is a very real obstacle for Reform
Even by the standards of their rivalry, the speed at which Rupert Lowe’s olive branch to Nigel Farage morphed into fresh recriminations between the two was swift.
It began with a softly lit 12-minute video posted on Sunday by the Restore Britain leader, looking straight to camera and referring to “Nigel” as he suggested his party could be willing to cast aside its differences with Reform UK and work together.

The Home Office has made a fresh request for ‘back door’ access to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users
Apple has launched a new legal challenge against a UK government demand to access its customers’ highly encrypted data, a year after the Home Office agreed to abandon its previous request.
The US tech company launched the legal complaint last month at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), an independent court that has the power to investigate claims that the UK intelligence services have acted unlawfully.

articles.title: Apple launches legal challenge against UK government demand to access data

Nigel Farage admits he discussed returning as Reform leader months before election, appearing to undermine previous claims
Nigel Farage has made his clearest admission that he was in talks to return to lead Reform UK months before the 2024 general election, casting fresh doubt on previous claims that he was not involved in politics when he received a £5m gift.
The admission will reopen questions about the nature of the gift – Farage has repeatedly insisted it was not linked to his political career since the Guardian first revealed it in April.

articles.title: Farage admission over timing of Reform leadership talks raises fresh doubts over £5m gift

articles.description:
Daniel was working at a market in Lagos when he was given the chance to start anew in the UK. He had no idea what was expected of him in return
• The summer issue of the Long Read magazine is out now. Click here to order
Daniel arrived in Lagos for the first time in 2016. He had come from a village in Ebonyi, a state in south-eastern Nigeria. He was 15 years old, the eldest of nine siblings, and his parents were farmers. When he was a boy, his father became sick and Daniel started working to assist his family, helping to cut trees and clear land. A few years later, he decided to seek his fortune in Lagos.
In Nigeria’s commercial capital, Daniel spent his days in the open-air Ikotun Market, where thousands of people shop every day for everything from tomatoes and fabric to suitcases and electronics. He sold cellphone accessories out of a wheelbarrow under a wide umbrella, making less than £10 a day. After living with a relative, he moved into a room with friends, including a young man named Chukwudi, who also worked in the market. Daniel had grown up in the same village as Chukwudi. A photo from their early childhood shows the boys together, Daniel in a red sportswear shirt.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The body snatchers: how a young Nigerian man was lured to London in an organ-trafficking plot

articles.description:
NatureScot refuses licence for hunt on Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir in which up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killed
A controversial Scottish seabird hunt will not go ahead for the first time in 400 years, in what campaigners have called a “victory for common sense”.
In the annual guga hunt, up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killed over a 10-day period on the uninhabited Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir, 40 miles north of Lewis and Harris.

articles.title: Scottish seabird hunt cancelled for first time in 400 years

articles.description:
Nigel Farage says he would use the military in the Channel but there are questions about whether the plan would work
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, whose summer has been dominated by the Guardian’s disclosure of a £5m undeclared gift and his connections with a fraudster, emerged on Monday to claim that his party would launch the “largest military operation in the English Channel since world war two” to prevent small boat crossings.

articles.title: Is Reform UK’s plan to use the navy to stop small boat crossings feasible?

Proposed $400bn tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb would create world’s fourth-largest drugmaker but analysts question rationale 
More than £17bn was wiped off the value of Britain’s biggest drugmaker, AstraZeneca, on Monday after a report that it was in discussions to take over its US rival Bristol Myers Squibb in a deal that would create a near $400bn (£300bn) pharmaceutical group.
AstraZeneca, run by Pascal Soriot, its longtime chief executive, had been worth nearly £196bn before the news broke. BMS, headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and known for its cancer treatments, was worth $133bn (£98bn).

articles.title: AstraZeneca shares fall 8.9% over merger talks with US cancer drug firm

England and Wales provisionally record driest July in nearly 200 years, Met Office says
July 2026 was the driest month in southern England since records began nearly 200 years ago, the Met Office has said.
England and Wales also provisionally recorded their driest July since records began in 1836. Wales had its joint warmest July on record for mean temperature, and England recorded its second warmest July.

articles.title: July was driest month in southern England since records began

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Attieh Fard and Andy Erlam make their byelection pitch to voters, but Reform UK’s leader is conspicuously absent
In the town square in Clacton, in the blazing midday sunshine, some of the candidates for the upcoming byelection made their pitch to a scattering of potential voters, passing Deliveroo drivers and a giant gull.

Party’s deputy leader says on social media the case is related to a complaint by an anti-Israel lobby group
UK politics live – latest updates
Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, is under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog over a possible failure to declare an interest.

articles.title: Standards watchdog investigating Reform UK’s Richard Tice

articles.author: Phillip Inman
articles.description:
Factories in upbeat mood despite fears over economic impact of US war on Iran, poll finds

Business live – latest updates

UK manufacturers ramped up production last month for the fourth consecutive month and at the fastest pace in almost two years, according to a leading survey of the industry.
The S&P Global poll of manufacturers found them in upbeat mood in July, though anxious about the prospect of a long war in the Middle East that would block supplies of oil and gas, and raise the cost of production.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK manufacturing growth picks up as Trump tariff chaos eases

articles.author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
articles.description:
Pop and rock legend tells Sunday Times of drinking problem and ill health after final Genesis tour in 2021
Phil Collins has said that he suffered life-threatening alcoholism in recent years.
Speaking to the Sunday Times, the pop and rock legend, 75, said that his drinking began after he stopped taking Antabuse, a drug that causes illness if alcohol is consumed, which he had been using since an earlier period of alcoholism.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Phil Collins details serious alcoholism: ‘People were coming to say goodbye’

Retired commander says policy lacks substance as party accused of trying to distract from Nigel Farage’s scandals
A Reform UK proposal to use the military to stop small boats bringing migrants to the UK from France lacks substance, a former Royal Navy officer has said, suggesting the UK’s warships would be better used countering actual military threats.
Reform’s political opponents have claimed its plans have more to do with distracting from the financial scandals surrounding its leader, Nigel Farage, than about solving the small boats issue, after the party proposed having the navy pick up people trying to make irregular Channel crossings and take them to France.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Former navy officer criticises Reform plan to use military to stop small boats

articles.author: Morgan Ofori and Kevin Rawlinson
articles.description:
Lowe says pair should put ‘personalities and our past disagreements aside for good of the country’
The leader of Restore Britain has extended an olive branch to Nigel Farage, saying the two should put “personalities and our past disagreements aside for the good of the country”.
Rupert Lowe told the Reform UK leader that if he was “prepared to work together around serious policies, serious reform and serious government, then so are we”.
Mass deportation of illegal migrants “including women and children”.
Tougher rules on legal migration, a ban on halal and kosher slaughter, the burqa, cousin marriage and sharia courts.
A referendum on the death penalty.
Welfare cuts to fund “self-sufficiency”.
The exclusion of former Tory ministers from any future cabinet.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rupert Lowe urges Nigel Farage to work with Restore Britain

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
Body providing care in east London and Bedfordshire accused of ‘unfathomable and unacceptable’ move
An NHS mental health trust plans to cut a wide range of its services and axe hundreds of jobs to close a £25m hole in its finances.
The move by the East London foundation trust (ELFT) and the scale of potential cuts involved have been called unfathomable given demand for NHS mental health support is rising rapidly.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS mental health trust plans £25m in cuts to jobs and services

articles.author: Sian Cain and agencies
articles.description:
Singer was due to reunite with Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in London production of Sunday in the Park With George
Ariana Grande has announced plans to take a break from public-facing work after her tour ends due to “endless, ongoing public scrutiny”. She is pulling out of the upcoming London revival of Sunday in the Park With George.
The pop singer was due to appear opposite her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in a new production of Stephen Sondheim’s critically acclaimed musical at the Barbican in 2027.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ariana Grande to take ‘a step back’ from public life due to ‘endless, ongoing scrutiny’

articles.author: Geneva Abdul
articles.description:
New Order and Simon Armitage among more than 100 signatories to criticise ‘foolish and shortsighted’ cuts
More than 100 artists, writers and scientists have called for the UK government to save the “world’s clearest eyes on the sky”, after funding for thenetwork of radio telescopes at Jodrell Bank Observatory was slashed.
New Order, the Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield and the poet laureate, Simon Armitage, are among those calling on the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, to save the deep space observatory which includes the Grade I-listed Lovell telescope, prized by astronomers who study galaxies, star formation and planets beyond the solar system.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Artists, writers and scientists urge UK government to save Jodrell Bank Observatory

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Decision comes after group of survivors claimed ex-Harrods owner’s associates must have helped facilitate his crimes
At least five victims of the former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed have been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of human trafficking.
A group of survivors of abuse by the deceased businessman had called for the Metropolitan police to make trafficking the main focus of its investigation, arguing that Fayed could not have committed his offences without a steady stream of women sent to him by associates.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: At least five Mohamed Al Fayed abuse survivors confirmed as human-trafficking victims

articles.author: Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Chancellor says the government wants to prevent shoppers being ‘taken for a ride’ at the pump or till 
The chancellor, John Healey, has said the government is standing by to prevent the public from “being taken for a ride at the pump or the till” as the Iran war continues to hit prices.
While he said there had been “no significant evidence of so-called price gouging” during the crisis, he used a weekend column to tell the big retailers that ministers were “watching closely” for any signs of profiteering.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Healey’s profiteering warning on food and fuel risks row with retailers

articles.title: Andy Burnham promises to be relentless in tackling small boat crossings – video

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Farmers battle to salvage what they can of their crops as heatwave set to continue
Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England, the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has warned as a heatwave was forecast to continue into next week.
The UK’s Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued heat health alerts for eight regions of England, with temperatures set to rise above 30C in parts of the country. UKHSA said rising temperatures may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Britain could face food shortages as drought continues, farmers warn

articles.author: Dalya Alberge
articles.description:
Exclusive: Outsourced guards, largely from minority ethnic backgrounds, barred from staff hub for mainly white employees
The National Gallery’s security staff, of whom the vast majority are from minority ethnic backgrounds, are facing shocking segregation, a senior curator has claimed.
Its outsourced guards are barred from the building’s high-quality “hub” – bright and airy recreation rooms that are available to the institution’s mainly white employees. They are not allowed to take their breaks there, or even sit in that area.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: National Gallery security staff segregated like ‘second-class citizens’, curator claims

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Volunteers painstakingly gather plastic pellets washing up on beaches after ship collision on 19 July
‘You’ve got a local community that really cares about the coastline,” said Alice Laverty, reflecting on the huge army of volunteers who had taken to crisis-hit beaches in north-east England with passion and only the most basic tools. “They’ve all got a dustpan, a brush, a bucket, a kitchen sieve.”
On beaches from Cambois in Northumberland to Seaburn on Wearside, up to 2,000 dedicated volunteers have been painstakingly sifting through sand to find tiny, lentil-sized pellets of plastic.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘There’s no nurdle fairy’: thousands mobilise to clean up plastic spillage in north-east England

articles.author: Bethan McKernan
articles.description:
Visible impact of warming climate is impossible to ignore across landscapes that have been starved of rainfall
Half of England and the whole of Wales are officially in drought and July is set to be the driest month on record as extreme heat intensified by the climate crisis continues to grip the UK and Europe this summer.
The announcements this week by England’s Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales mark the third such event over the past five years, and come in the wake of four record-breaking heatwaves since May which have fuelled huge wildfires and left farmers, wildlife and protected habitats running out of water.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Relentless UK heatwaves turn ‘green and pleasant land’ brown

articles.author: Aisha Down, Dan Milmo and Graeme Wearden
articles.description:
Investors scramble to make sense of a shock Chinese challenge to the dominance of western chipmakers
Even for the rollercoaster world of AI, last week was particularly volatile as investors scrambled to keep up with developments that threatened the dominance of the largest western chipmakers.
It began with a double whammy. On Monday, the Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT floated on the Shanghai stock market, soaring by 466% in value to 3.3tn yuan (£365bn).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stock market turmoil sheds stark light on the opaque AI economy

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Britons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choice
If you manage to spot a garden in bloom this summer, beyond the strips of bleached and torched grass, there may be one colour you see more than any other: purple, the horticultural hue of the season.
Plants such as lavender, salvias and catmint are in vogue, according to the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS), which conducted extensive research into the colours Britons best love to see in their gardens.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Purple reign: how shade became British gardeners’ favourite

articles.author: Kevin Rawlinson
articles.description:
Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problem
If you believe rightwing influencers and politicians, Dover and the wider Kent coast has been the site of an “invasion” for years now. And, for an online audience of millions, they and their camera crews have been the vanguard in the nation’s defence.
Indeed, if you believe all you see on the algorithms of amateur Channel watchers, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, braved a hail of French gunfire as he took to the water in a fishing boat this week; an attempt by the French authorities, he suggested, to deter him in his mission of highlighting the small boats crisis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: On the ground in the English seaside town rightwing influencers say is being ‘invaded’

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Labour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadership
Extraordinarily, given the importance of geopolitics, the office of foreign secretary has sometimes appeared a consolation prize in British politics, perhaps reflecting the transfer of responsibility to Downing Street or the Cabinet Office.
That is not how Ed Miliband views the job. His allies say suggestions that he nurses resentment after he was deprived of the chance to be chancellor misunderstand his grasp of the policy challenges ahead. “Ed has an immense appetite to get things done and is relishing being in this job,” one says. “Ed will be a policy-driven foreign secretary.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: EU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challenges

articles.author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
articles.description:
Duetting stars surpass record set in 1953, when crooner Frankie Laine hit the top with I Believe
Sam Fender and Olivia Dean have scored the longest running UK No 1 single in history with Rein Me In, beating a record that has stood since 1953.
Back then, the UK singles chart had been running for less than a year and contained just 12 songs when I Believe, a bombastic ballad by US crooner Frankie Laine, hit No 1 and spent a total of 18 weeks on the chart.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In breaks 73-year record to become longest-running UK No 1 single

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Exclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too late
The bereaved daughter of a British couple who died in a Spanish wildfire is calling on the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to get answers from Spain’s government about why her parents were not told to evacuate until it was too late.
Severe wildfires have burned across Spain and France since early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Daughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leave

articles.author: Peter Apps, Robert Booth, Sarah Ann Harris and Lauren Hurrell
articles.description:
A Guardian investigation has revealed that a political lobbying firm, founded by the former electoral strategist for David Cameron and Boris Johnson, secretly pays journalists to write pieces for British newspapers that are favourable to its clients.
In a practice that appears to create a back door for private companies to influence public opinion, lobbyists for CT Group, which was co-founded by the campaign strategist Lynton Crosby, told an undercover reporter they had paid journalists to place apparently independent stories in newspapers.
In a statement, CT Group said: 'We do not comment publicly on work we do for clients and we therefore cannot respond to the specific allegations you have made.' CT Group said the events had been 'deliberately mischaracterised' and it did not engage the undercover journalist to do anything and did not pay him anything. It said the journalist was looking for work and 'chased us relentlessly over a period of more than six months'


Lobbying giant filmed offering reporter payment for flattering client coverage in national press

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why undercover footage exposing lobbyists raises concerns for journalism – video explainer

articles.description:
More than 100 firefighters have been battling a blaze on Dunwich Heath, near Leiston on the Suffolk coast, since Wednesday evening and the situation is 'stabilising'. About 50 people have been evacuated from their homes and a nearby holiday park, with some being moved to Westleton, where the village hall was turned into a rest centre


Suffolk wildfire near Sizewell nuclear plant ‘stabilising’ after 24 hours

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Evacuees from Suffolk fire reflect on 'incredibly emotional' day – video

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
Scheme brought in up to 500 foreign-trained doctors a year and was seen as example of British ‘soft power’
The NHS has scrapped a longstanding scheme that let overseas doctors boost their skills in UK hospitals and was seen as an example of British “soft power”.
Senior doctors have criticised NHS England’s decision to axe the Medical Training Initiative, under which 400 to 500 foreign-trained doctors were given placements in Britain every year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Medical colleges condemn scrapping of NHS placements for overseas doctors

articles.author: Written by Patrick Barkham and read by Dermot Daly. Produced by Nicola Alexandrou. The executive producer was Madeleine Finlay
articles.description:
Intensive farming has all but destroyed England’s ancient woodlands and freshwater wetlands. On a farm in Lincolnshire a radical aristocrat hopes to show there’s money in protecting nature
By Patrick Barkham. Read by Dermot Daly

articles.title: ‘It makes your heart sing’: can a pioneering project show that rewilding really works? – podcast

articles.author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Peter Walker, produced by Frankie Tobi, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj.
articles.description:
Andy Burnham gave a major speech on Wednesday on his plans for a national care service. He sought cross-party consensus on the issue by speaking to the Tories and Lib Dems. But not Reform UK or the Greens. On Thursday, Reform’s Robert Jenrick claimed at a press conference that the prime minister wanted a ‘death tax’. But is that what Burnham set out?
